Nell's here now. Nell Holloway. Forty years since she told me about the marker, and neither of us has spoken of it since. Now she's in my kitchen wanting bread, and I'm to take baskets to the field.

Marta's given the order—east strip, now, with the boys. Nell's here, and I'm to pretend I don't know what I know. The same as every day for forty years.

Corwin asked me about the lumber yard, but Marta's cut through it. Harvest first, timber after. She's right. Bellies before business. Let me answer Corwin brief and get to the field. Burlap answer. Send him on his way to help Wren. If he goes, I can stay and watch Nell a moment, or go with and keep my distance. 

Better to move. Standing still with Nell in the room costs nothing but tension. Let Corwin go ahead, and I'll follow. No need to be in the same breath as Nell Holloway any longer than the work demands. </think>  Let Corwin go ahead. I'll follow once I've got the lay of the morning. </think> Let Corwin go ahead. Marta has given the order—east strip, baskets, not timber talk. My nephew will head down to help Wren cut wheat. I will go after, once I've seen who else moves and who stays still.

Nell Holloway stands with coin for bread and four decades of silence between us. She has never asked again, and I have never told. A promise outlasts the reason, but it does not outlast hunger. If her household lacks bread, that is one thing. If she has coin to pay, that is another. I watch what people do with their hands when their mouths say something else.

I will get to the field before the wheat lies too long in the wet.
